collection.description: Overnight, a market stall has appeared at the edge of the village.

ask.text:
Overnight, a market stall has appeared at the edge of the village. It's made of driftwood and woven palm, with its wares laid out on a red cloth: little glass bottles, carved wooden boxes, tiny figures of birds and fish. A small bell hangs from the roof, without a clapper.
There's no merchant in sight. No sign, no prices, nothing. Just the goods, waiting. A small crowd has gathered, but nobody wants to be the first to touch anything. (Name) is standing closest. What should (he/she) do?

c1o1.text: The bottle holds a fragrant golden oil that smells of flowers and honey. The healers test a drop and are delighted: it's wonderful for soothing cracked, sore skin. Within a week, every fisher with chapped hands is begging (name) for a dab. When the bottle runs dry, the healers try very hard to copy it, but never quite manage.

c1o2.text: The moment (name) picks it up, the clear liquid inside turns cloudy, swirling grey like a storm in a jar. (Name) watches it swirl for a moment, then sets it carefully aside. (He/She) isn't about to put that on (his/her) skin. Or in (his/her) mouth. Or anywhere. It sits on a shelf, cloudy forever.

c1.text: (Name) leaves a handful of shells on the red cloth, as fair payment, and picks up one of the little bottles...

c2o1.text: Inside is a bundle of preserved herbs, dried and tied with grass, still fragrant: wild ginger, lemon leaf and something peppery nobody recognizes. The cooks are thrilled. They add a pinch to everything for weeks, and the village eats better than it has in ages. Your villagers gain (award) food.

c2o2.text: Inside is a single folded piece of bark with a message on it. (Name) unfolds it, and goes cold. It's written in (his/her) own handwriting. Unmistakably. The message says: "You already know." (Name) has no memory of writing it. (He/She) has no idea what (he/she) already knows. (He/She) keeps the note anyway, folded in (his/her) pocket, and takes it out to read sometimes.

c2.text: (Name) leaves a few shells and picks up one of the little carved boxes. It's light. Something inside shifts as (he/she) turns it...

c3o1.text: After a while, an elderly traveler comes hobbling up the path with an armful of fresh wares. "Oh! Customers!" The old one explains that (he/she) set up before sunrise, then wandered off to find breakfast, and lost track of time chatting with some fishers. (He/She) is very pleased to have someone waiting, and gives (name) a little carved fish for (his/her) patience.

c3o2.text: (Name) waits all morning. The merchant doesn't come. Around midday, thirsty, (name) gets up to fetch water from the well, just for a moment. When (he/she) comes back, the stall is gone: the driftwood, the palm, the red cloth, the bottles, the boxes, all of it. There's not even a mark on the ground where it stood.

c3.text: (Name) sits down beside the stall to wait. Surely the merchant will be back soon...

c4o1.text: By evening, the stall is gone. No one saw anyone take it down. No one saw a merchant come or go. There's not a single trace that it was ever there, except the memory of it, which the villagers discuss endlessly over supper.

c4o2.text: By evening, the stall is gone. But lying on the ground where it stood is a small carved bird, apparently forgotten. It's carved from pale wood, with a tiny beak and closed eyes, and it fits neatly in the palm. (Name) picks it up. It feels as though it was left there on purpose. (He/She) keeps it by (his/her) bed.

c4.text: (Name) decides that goods without an owner aren't goods (he/she) wants to take. (He/She) tells the others to leave the stall alone...
